Julius, thank you for the quote. But six percent more is a lot. Our board won’t accept a price increase like that.
I understand, Anna. But steel is twenty percent more expensive this year. We can’t absorb the cost alone.
What if we increased the volume? We could order fifteen thousand parts instead of ten.
That helps. If you made a commitment to fifteen thousand, we would reduce the increase to four percent.
Four is still too high. Can we meet halfway at three?
Three is possible, provided that you sign a long-term contract for three years.
And the payment terms? We need ninety days. Sixty is a deal-breaker for us.
We can accept ninety days, as long as there’s a surcharge clause. Unless steel prices fall, we’ll review the price in six months.

I've been a purchasing manager in Detroit for eighteen years, and every year some suppliers ask me for a higher price. That's normal. Costs go up. What matters is how they ask. My first question is always the same. Show me the numbers. Which costs went up, and by how much? If a supplier shows me the numbers, I usually accept part of the increase. We talk, we meet somewhere in the middle, and we keep working together. But some suppliers just send a new price list with no explanation. If a supplier surprised me like that, I would start looking for another supplier the same week. Not because of the money, but because of the trust. A good supplier tells you early, explains clearly, and offers something in return.

I teach negotiation to managers in Paris, Lyon and sometimes Sao Paulo, and in every course I teach one rule before anything else. Never give something without getting something back. When a customer asks for a discount, most people simply say yes or no. Both answers are weak. A good negotiator says, yes, provided that you sign for two years. Or, we can do that if you pay in thirty days. You give, but you also get. I also love the word unless. Unless we receive the order this week, we can't guarantee the price. It's polite, it's clear, and it sets a limit without any aggression. In French we say that the conditions make the deal, and I think it's true in every language.

A few years ago, the price of aluminum went up by almost thirty percent in six months. We supplied wheels to a large customer in Germany, and we had to ask for a higher price. The meeting in Munich was terrible. They refused any increase, and after two hours we had nothing. Everybody was tired and a little angry. Then their purchasing director invited me for a coffee after the meeting, just the two of us. And there, in ten minutes, we found a solution. They accepted half of the increase, provided that the price was reviewed every six months. If prices came down, the increase would disappear. Since that day, I never leave a difficult meeting without asking for a coffee.
